title: What is a database sequence (`CREATE SEQUENCE`, `nextval`), how does it differ from an identity/auto-increment column (a sequence is independent of a table — reusable, multi-table, gapless optional; identity is table-bound), and why do sequences have gaps (caching, rollbacks) which is normal and expected?

s1_definition.profdef: A database sequence is a standalone object that generates a monotonically increasing series of numbers on demand via `nextval`, created with `CREATE SEQUENCE`. It is independent of any table, so it can be shared across multiple tables and controlled explicitly. An identity or auto-increment column is a column-level feature that binds a generator directly to one table's column and fills it automatically on insert. Sequences develop gaps — because values are cached per session and because a rolled-back or conflicting transaction still consumes its drawn value — and this is normal and expected, since sequences guarantee uniqueness and increasing order, not contiguity.
s1_definition.analogy: A sequence is like a central ticket machine in National Bank of India's lobby: anyone from any counter can pull the next ticket number, and the numbers only ever go up. An identity column is like a ticket roll bolted to one specific counter — convenient, but it only serves that counter. Gaps happen because a customer who pulls ticket 51 and then leaves without being served still spent ticket 51; the machine never reissues it, so you later see 50, then 52. That is by design — the machine promises unique, rising numbers, not a perfectly unbroken run.
s1_definition.oneliner: A sequence is a standalone, shareable number generator; identity binds one to a single table's column — and both gap on caching and rollbacks because they promise uniqueness and order, not contiguity.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A database sequence is a standalone object that generates a monotonically increasing series of numbers on demand via `nextval`, created with `CREATE SEQUENCE`. It is independent of any table, so it can be shared across multiple tables and controlled explicitly. An identity or auto-increment column is a column-level feature that binds a generator directly to one table's column and fills it automatically on insert. Sequences develop gaps — because values are cached per session and because a rolled-back or conflicting transaction still consumes its drawn value — and this is normal and expected, since sequences guarantee uniqueness and increasing order, not contiguity.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A sequence is like a central ticket machine in National Bank of India's lobby: anyone from any counter can pull the next ticket number, and the numbers only ever go up. An identity column is like a ticket roll bolted to one specific counter — convenient, but it only serves that counter. Gaps happen because a customer who pulls ticket 51 and then leaves without being served still spent ticket 51; the machine never reissues it, so you later see 50, then 52. That is by design — the machine promises unique, rising numbers, not a perfectly unbroken run.

**One line to remember:** A sequence is a standalone, shareable number generator; identity binds one to a single table's column — and both gap on caching and rollbacks because they promise uniqueness and order, not contiguity.

sections.s2_technical:
A sequence is created with CREATE SEQUENCE and you draw values with nextval, inspect the last value in your session with currval, and jump it with setval. Because it is a separate object, several tables can share one sequence — useful when you want globally unique ids across related tables — and you can configure its start, increment, minimum, maximum, cycling, and cache size. You can also call nextval in application logic before inserting, so you know the id you are about to use.

An identity column (the SQL-standard GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY) or an auto-increment column (MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT, older PostgreSQL serial) is a convenience that attaches a generator to exactly one column of one table and populates it automatically on insert. Under the hood PostgreSQL's serial and identity are still backed by a sequence, but the binding is table-local and managed for you. You do not share it across tables, and with GENERATED ALWAYS you cannot even supply your own value.

The key differences are independence and control. A sequence is reusable and multi-table and gives you explicit control via nextval and setval; identity is table-bound and automatic. Choose a shared sequence when multiple tables need ids from one pool or when the application needs the id before the insert; choose identity for the simple, common case of one table filling its own primary key.

Gaps are inherent to both for two reasons. First, caching: for performance a session or node grabs a block of sequence values at once — say fifty — and hands them out locally; any values left unused when the session ends are discarded, creating gaps. Second, rollbacks and conflicts: a transaction that drew a value and then rolled back, or an upsert whose insert turned into an update, still consumed its value, because sequences are non-transactional and never give values back. This is intentional: making a sequence gapless would require serializing every insert through a single lock, destroying concurrency.

The senior nuance: never rely on contiguity. Do not use the maximum id as a row count, do not assume id+1 is the next row, and if you truly need a legally gapless series like invoice numbers, use a dedicated counter row updated inside the transaction and accept the contention, or post-process numbering separately.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India wants globally unique reference numbers shared across both transfer records and loan records, and must understand why the numbers are not contiguous.

Problem 1 — one shared pool across tables. We model a single sequence that both a TransferService and a LoanService draw from, so the reference numbers are globally unique across both tables.

Problem 2 — identity is table-bound. We contrast with a table-local identity generator that only serves its own table.

Problem 3 — gaps from caching and rollback. We model a cached sequence that discards unused cached values at session end, and a rolled-back draw that is never returned, both producing visible gaps.

The code includes a Sequence with configurable cache, a TableIdentity bound to one table, services that draw from the shared sequence, and a demo showing shared ids and gaps.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
sequence-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/main/java/com/bank/sequence/
│   ├── SequenceDemo.java
│   ├── gen/Sequence.java
│   ├── gen/TableIdentity.java
│   └── service/ReferenceService.java
└── src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_tables.sql
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
CREATE SEQUENCE ref_seq START 1 INCREMENT 1 CACHE 50;   -- shared, cached → gaps possible

CREATE TABLE transfers (
    ref_no  BIGINT PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT nextval('ref_seq'),  -- draws from shared sequence
    amount  DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE loans (
    ref_no  BIGINT PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT nextval('ref_seq'),  -- SAME shared sequence
    principal DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

-- Table-bound identity (serves only this table):
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
    id      BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    message VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL
);

-- Draw a value in app logic before inserting:
-- SELECT nextval('ref_seq');
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
sequence:
  cache-size: 50     # values cached per session; unused ones become gaps
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a shared sequence with cache size 50, drawn by both transfers and loans, plus a rollback and a session end.

Step 1 — The first transfer draws ref_no 1 from the shared sequence. The loan then draws ref_no 2 from the very same pool, proving one sequence can feed multiple tables with globally unique ids. A second transfer draws 3.

Step 2 — A transaction draws ref_no 4 and then rolls back. Because the sequence is non-transactional, 4 is never returned to the pool.

Step 3 — The next transfer draws ref_no 5, so the stored ids jump 3 then 5, leaving a gap at 4 from the rollback.

Step 4 — A separate table-bound identity generates id 1 for the audit log, completely independent of the shared sequence, showing identity is table-local.

Step 5 — The session ends while the cached block still held values 6 through 50. Those cached-but-unused values are discarded, creating a large gap before the next session's block. Both gap causes — rollback and caching — are now demonstrated.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [INFO] === Shared sequence across two tables ===
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [INFO] transfer ref_no=1
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [INFO] loan ref_no=2 (same pool as transfers)
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [INFO] transfer ref_no=3
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [INFO] === Rollback causes a gap ===
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [WARNING] drew ref_no=4 then ROLLBACK → value lost (GAP)
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [INFO] transfer ref_no=5
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [INFO] === Table-bound identity is separate ===
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [INFO] audit_log id=1 (independent of ref_seq)
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [INFO] === Caching gap at session end ===
2026-10-25 17:41:00 [WARNING] session end → discarding cached values 6..50 (GAP)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Sequence vs Identity ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Shared generator (sequence) vs bound generator (identity) │
  │  Block caching for throughput (trade: gaps)                │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─ SOLID ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Sequence generates; services consume.                  │
  │  D: services depend on Sequence abstraction, shareable.    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ Sequence                 │◀───────│ ReferenceService      │
  │ - global/cache cursor    │ uses   │ + newTransferRef()    │
  │ + nextval(): long        │        │ + newLoanRef()        │
  │ + endSession() (gaps)    │        │ + rolledBackDraw()    │
  └──────────────────────────┘        └───────────────────────┘
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ TableIdentity            │  table-local only (not shared)
  │ + nextForThisTableOnly() │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. newTransferRef→1, newLoanRef→2, newTransferRef→3  (shared pool)
  2. rolledBackDraw→4 lost, newTransferRef→5           (gap at 4)
  3. audit identity→1                                   (independent)
  4. endSession → discard 6..50                         (cache gap)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A database sequence is a standalone object that generates a monotonically increasing series of numbers on demand. I create it with CREATE SEQUENCE and draw values with nextval, and because it is independent of any table I can share one sequence across several tables, call nextval from application logic before I even insert, and control its start, increment, and caching explicitly. An identity or auto-increment column is instead a column-level convenience that binds a generator to exactly one table's column and fills it automatically on insert. In PostgreSQL the serial and identity types are actually backed by a sequence under the hood, but the binding is table-local and managed for me, and with GENERATED ALWAYS I cannot even supply my own value.

So the difference comes down to independence and control. A sequence is reusable, multi-table, and explicitly controllable, which I choose when several tables need ids from one pool or when I need the id before the insert. Identity is table-bound and automatic, which I choose for the ordinary case of one table filling its own primary key.

Both develop gaps, and this is normal and expected rather than a bug. Two things cause gaps. First, caching: for throughput a session grabs a whole block of values at once, and any left unused when the session ends are simply discarded. Second, rollbacks and conflicts: a transaction that drew a value and then rolled back, or an upsert whose insert became an update, still consumed its value, because sequences are non-transactional and never hand values back. Making a sequence gapless would mean serializing every insert through one lock and killing concurrency, so the engine deliberately trades contiguity for speed. In our National Bank of India system we share one sequence across transfer and loan reference numbers for global uniqueness, and we see gaps from both caching and rolled-back draws. The rules I follow are to never treat ids as contiguous, never use the maximum id as a row count, and when I genuinely need a legally gapless series like an invoice number, use a dedicated counter row updated inside the transaction and accept the contention. The line I remember is that a sequence is a standalone, shareable number generator while identity binds one to a single table's column, and both gap on caching and rollbacks because they guarantee uniqueness and order, not an unbroken run.
